title: A defence-in-depth strategy for securing AI-driven biological sequence design - Nature Communications
byline: Sprang; Maximilian; Hassan Ahmed; Ektefaie; Yasha; Schmieder; Anne; Wasilenko; Alix; Hanke; Moritz S; Martín-Peña; Rosa E; Harkness; Rachael; Götting; Jasper; M
html:
Abstract

Generative artificial intelligence can design biological sequences, from proteins to whole genomes, opening opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, but the same capability can be misused. The Wübben Sandpit conference brought together experts in biology, AI, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy to ask how the field can capture the benefits while managing the risks. Here we set out a defence-in-depth strategy that builds safeguards into every stage, from the data used to train models, to the models themselves, to the synthesis of physical DNA. We argue that responsible governance is not a brake on progress but a precondition for it.

Introduction

The life sciences are undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift, transitioning from a descriptive discipline to one driven by predictive engineering. This transformation is driven by the convergence of high-throughput measurement and engineering platforms, such as nanopore long-read sequencing, gene editing and the industrialisation of wet-lab automation. A key outcome of this convergence is the sharp, exponential decline in genomic sequencing costs, which has triggered a data explosion that far exceeds the analytical capacity of traditional heuristic and statistical methods.

This deluge of information is at the heart of the tensions and opportunities of modern biotechnology, and is the primary impetus for the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for Biological Sequences’ Wübben Sandpit conference. While AI offers unprecedented capabilities for biological discovery, the same pattern-recognition architectures that decode life’s complexity also pose significant biosecurity risks. Navigating this landscape requires striking a balance between fostering rapid innovation and implementing robust safeguards against the accidental or intentional misuse of GenAI for biological sequence design.

In this work, we focus on generative sequence models as a subcomponent of biological AI. These are systems that are trained on large corpora of proteins or nucleic acids at the genome scale. They learn the statistical structure of biological sequences and can generate new ones. Their near-term promise is tangible. Such models have already designed functional proteins, enzymes and high-affinity binders, and small viral genomes, with applications ranging from bespoke bacteriophages against antimicrobial resistance to faster design of therapeutics and medical countermeasures1,2,3,4,5,6.

These capabilities are advancing quickly, as improving architectures and the industrialisation of synthesis compress the design-build-test cycle. A structural asymmetry accompanies this progress: in silico generation now far outpaces the throughput of physical synthesis and validation, so models can propose sequences faster than they can be screened or tested. The same generative power that enables beneficial design also lowers the barrier to misuse7, and this dual-use tension is the central concern of this Perspective.

We set out the dual-use risks of biological sequence design and propose a defence-in-depth framework spanning the governance of training data, models and nucleic acid synthesis, summarised in Table 1. While recent work has addressed individual aspects of this challenge, including tiered data governance8 and a review of the risk landscape9, the present work provides an integrated set of recommendations covering the entire biological risk chain, from data to models to synthesis, with a particular focus on the European context.

This Perspective consolidates the discussions of the Wübben Sandpit conference, a 3-day interdisciplinary workshop held from 25 to 27 November 2025 at Wasem Kloster Engelthal, Germany and funded by the Wübben Wissenschaftsstiftung. The workshop brought together twenty participants spanning molecular biology, artificial intelligence, bioinformatics, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy, drawn from academia, industry, applied research and government across Europe and the United States, together with two neutral facilitators. It followed a design-thinking format that moved iteratively from problem space to solution space through alternating rounds of divergence and convergence, combining facilitated small-group work, structured brainstorming, clustering and prioritisation exercises, and plenary synthesis. Participants first mapped the translational barriers and dual-use risks of generative AI for biological sequence design, and then drafted candidate recommendations, each linked explicitly to the barrier or risk it addressed, its intended audience, and its dependencies. These drafts were stress-tested by rotating participants between groups and by probing how each recommendation might be circumvented, fail in practice, or disadvantage under-resourced actors, and were then prioritised through participant voting on perceived importance and feasibility. No formal consensus vote was taken; the recommendations presented here are the directions that emerged from these discussions, consolidated and refined by the authors after the workshop.

Near-term dual-use risks of biological sequence design

As these capabilities advance and models become more widely available, they create new dual-use risks that must be anticipated and governed.

In this section, we provide an overview of the dual-use risks associated with these models, from data collection and trained models to sequence synthesis and potential deployment in physical and biological systems (Table 2). Risk originates at the data level. Any information about sequence-to-function data, particularly that which includes pathogenic or toxic sequences, can be used by malicious actors to train or fine-tune models that can design sequences with potentially harmful functions. When using pre-trained models, a large number of annotated sequences is not required. In their 2025 study, King et al. fine-tuned a genome language model on around 14,000 Microviridae genomes and generated variants of the small (~5.4 kb) ΦX174 bacteriophage genome; after extensive computational and experimental filtering, 16 of 285 synthesised designs were viable, infectious phages at 93–99% nucleotide identity to their nearest natural genomes5. This calls into question one of the major obstacles to utilising public data, as effective labelling is required and recommended, despite the possibility for dual usage. Funding bodies and researchers must play an active role in deciding which data should be withheld from the public if it includes dangerous sequences or sequence information. However, genomes of viruses that are considered high risk for misuse as biological weapons and those that have led to global pandemics are already in the public domain10. Another issue that will be mentioned repeatedly across different domains is the circumvention of security safeguards, as pathogenic data could be used to adversarially fine-tune pre-trained models that did not contain pathogens in their training corpus11.

The general availability of genomic data lowers the barrier to training and designing models for all actors, enabling small laboratories and, potentially, malicious ones; large, high-capability models work similarly. Key actors here are researchers who open-source data and state actors that provide training infrastructure. Open-sourcing encourages collaboration and accelerates innovation, but this must be weighed against the associated threats12,13. Therefore, it is important to differentiate between what such models have demonstrated already from what remains theoretical, albeit plausible. To date, generative models have been shown to design functional proteins and interaction complexes, enzyme active sites and small, template-anchored viral genomes and operons, validated in benign laboratory systems1,2,3,4,5,6. In parallel, sequence models can already predict the fitness and immune-escape potential of viral variants in silico14,15,16, the same properties that gain-of-function studies probe experimentally. Biorisk evaluations find that such virus-relevant capability is present in open-weight genome models and is not reliably removed by filtering their training data7,17. What has not been demonstrated is the de novo design of enhanced human pathogens, deliberate host-range expansion, or gene drives. However, substantial barriers remain between generating a viable sequence and achieving a defined biological function, pathogenicity and real-world deployment. The concern we address is that continued progress could enable such capabilities over time, not that current models can already produce weaponised agents. A designed organism first needs to be synthesised in order to be introduced to the environment.

This process would need to involve process engineers, biochemists, commercial synthesis providers, or contract research organisations (CROs). The latter are particularly influenced by the governance framework in which they operate, which varies greatly between countries. While many synthesis companies do screen sequences sent to them for harmful ones using various technical measures, this is not mandatory in many countries (for current provider-level screening commitments, see, for example, the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security list of providers attesting to the U.S. Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening18. Additionally, sequence-similarity screening is moreover increasingly challenged by AI-designed variants, motivating a shift towards function-based screening19).

Finally, these capabilities raise the question of deliberate misuse, which spans scenarios that differ greatly in feasibility, in the actors capable of realising them, and in the contribution of GenAI. At the more tractable end, models could assist in designing protein toxins; far more demanding are the enhancement of infectious agents, the creation of host-specific pathogens for agricultural or ecological harm, and, in the most severe case, agents with pandemic potential. Most of these outcomes remain well beyond demonstrated capability and depend on tacit knowledge and physical resources that lone actors are more likely to lack. The concern is not that any single model already enables them, but that GenAI could lower barriers at several points along the biological risk chain (Fig. 1), with a contribution that differs from step to step. As noted above, models may also assist with the design and circumvention of safeguards and with experimental design and laboratory work20,21,22,23.

The four main events relevant for biosequence modelling are shown. When used independently, they cause little to no harm. However, a threat emerges when they occur in sequence. 1. Generative AI (GenAI) is transforming synthetic biology by enabling the design of novel 'new-to-nature' sequences, including complete genomes and proteins such as toxins, which could have different properties from naturally evolved organisms. These tools are trained on vast genetic datasets in order to learn the 'grammar' of life and create functional sequences that might bypass existing biosecurity safeguards in nucleic acid synthesis screening. 2. Gain-of-function (GOF) research involves altering an organism’s genome to enhance its existing abilities or confer new ones. These new abilities may include improved transmissibility, virulence, or host range. Examples of observed GOF at different molecular levels include modifying DNA/genomes to alter pathogen stability or virulence, engineering RNA to enhance replication or immune evasion, and mutating proteins to strengthen host interactions or expression patterns. With increasing model capabilities, more of this work could be done purely in silico, further accelerating the process depicted here. 3. Synthesising these sequences is how they go from digital to physical substrate. While most synthesis providers have implemented safeguards against misuse, these are not mandatory and can vary considerably between countries and providers. Furthermore, GenAI can be exploited to circumvent these safeguards. For instance, new-to-nature sequences are unlikely to be recognised by methods designed to detect known pathogens. Models can also be used to conceal a gain-of-function mutation by shuffling the sequence or employing alternative codons to encode a target protein. 4. Creation of biological agents or molecular carriers, which are then disseminated into the environment by a malicious actor. Depending on the malicious actor’s scope and goals, these could be targeted pathogens or pandemic agents.

Strategic recommendations for mitigating dual-use research of concern risks in generative AI for biological sequence design

Throughout the Sandpit conference, participants converged on the view that mitigating dual-use risks inherent in the computational design of genomic sequences requires a defence-in-depth architecture. Rather than relying on a single point of control, the proposed framework takes a layered approach that covers all parts of the risk chain, from the initial curation of data and training of models to the final biological synthesis of sequence outputs.

A key principle of these recommendations is that governance must be dynamic and iterative. As Genomic GenAI capabilities advance at an unprecedented rate, classification systems and access controls must undergo regular technical audits. Participants identified ’upstream’ levers, specifically funding mandates and data-sharing agreements, as the most effective instruments for embedding responsible practices before high-risk sequences reach the synthesis stage.

Although the objective is protective, these recommendations acknowledge certain operational limitations to ensure that security measures do not inadvertently impede legitimate research. To prevent a 'bottleneck effect' on public health research or pandemic preparedness, we propose a tiered-access model. Moving away from a binary ‘open vs. closed’ data philosophy, we support a risk-stratified environment. For data, we build on the tiered scheme of Bloomfield et al.8, which sorts biological data into five biosecurity data levels (BDL-0 to BDL-4) according to the capability it could confer on a model trained on it. We summarise these levels, and the platform that would host the data, in Recommendation 3.

With such an approach, governance can be a facilitator of secure innovation. The shift towards structured oversight in biological sequence design is supported by successful applications in related high-stakes biological fields, as well as by successes in data management, software security and industrial manufacturing (see the overarching justifications below;8,24,25). The two boxes below collect points that recurred throughout the Sandpit discussions and that touch multiple recommendations within the three domains (data, models or synthesis). The justifications are precedents to mechanisms that transfer between domains: tiered access and red-teaming, for example, serve both data and models, and risk-scoring methods developed for data can be repurposed to score de novo sequences. The limitations are the concerns that likewise apply across multiple recommendations or are general problems of risk classification and mitigation in unknown frontiers and could be brought up against suggestions such as tiered access.

Overarching justifications

  • Data tiering (the provenance precedent): the UK Biobank and other similar repositories show that providing controlled access to sensitive genomic information improves data standardisation and documentation. This structured approach increases the resource’s utility for the global research community while maintaining strict privacy and security safeguards.

  • Model Red-Teaming (The AI Safety Precedent): in the broader AI domain, ‘gated release’ and adversarial red-teaming have become standard practice for high-capability models (e.g. Frontier Model Forum protocols). Applying these practices to GenAI in biological sequence design enables the identification of potential biological risks, such as a model’s capacity to design novel pathogens, before the weights are made publicly accessible.

  • Synthesis screening (The Physical-Gatekeeping Precedent): The International Gene Synthesis Consortium (IGSC) has already established a successful, industry-led screening framework for physical DNA orders26. Expanding these protocols to include more sophisticated, AI-generated sequence variants ensures that the ’digital-to-biological’ bridge is monitored by robust, standardised biosecurity checks.

  • Institutional synthesis: rather than proposing overly complex new regulations, these recommendations are designed to integrate with existing institutional review processes and funding requirements. This approach minimises administrative friction while maximising compliance across the research lifecycle.
